title: Training Agentic Reasoners — Will Brown, Prime Intellect

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling

summary: Will Brown frames the talk around the thesis that reasoning and agents are fundamentally the same thing, unified through RL. RL now works at scale: DeepSeek showed RL applied at scale with surprisingly few tweaks, and big labs like OpenAI (o3) are doubling down on RL compute. Agent products (Claude Code, Devon, Manis, o3, Deep Research) succeed because their models were likely RL'd in similar agentic settings. Building agents maps to canonical RL: policies, actions, states, rewards, transition probabilities; tuning prompts and harnesses is 'RL by hand.' RL algorithms estimate advantage from branching rollouts. GRPO is praised as a practical middle ground—computationally efficient, simple, with forking via sampling—while DPO lacks fine-grained advantage and PPO is accurate but expensive. Brown cautions against chasing papers with sensationalist titles and instead focusing on tools, environments, and real problems. Most RL codebases are set up for math and code because those are easy to evaluate, but real-world tasks are messier. Reward hacking is a core challenge: the key principle is making the eval easier to do honestly than to hack, so models flow along the path of least resistance toward the task itself. Brown highlights rubric-based evaluation—using LLMs as subroutines, including DeepSeek's work on reward models that generate rubrics on the fly—as a promising direction for ambiguous tasks. Multi-turn agentic systems (tool calls, software, games, long-horizon planning, computer use, memory) are where things are headed. Brown introduces his open-source 'verifiers' library, which lets you build agents trainable with RL using an OpenAI-compatible API in a standard while-loop. A Wordle agent demo on a 7B model illustrates the approach, with rewards for solving and efficiency. SFT warm-up from synthetic data generated by frontier APIs lowers the barrier for small models. The library handles async training and off-policy execution so users need only a couple of GPUs to experiment.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Reasoning and agents are fundamentally the same thing, unified through RL; prompt and harness tuning is 'RL by hand.'
RL now works at scale—DeepSeek and o3 are proof; big labs are betting on RL compute for future progress.
Agent products (Claude Code, Devon, Manis, o3, Deep Research) succeed because their models were RL-trained in similar agentic settings.
GRPO is a practical middle ground: efficient, simple, with forking via sampling; DPO lacks fine-grained advantage; PPO is accurate but expensive.
Reward hacking is fundamentally an eval design problem: make doing the task honestly easier than gaming the eval; models follow the path of least resistance.
Rubric-based evaluation using LLMs as subroutines (including DeepSeek's on-the-fly rubric generation) is a promising direction for ambiguous, real-world tasks.
Multi-turn agentic systems—tool calls, software, games, long-horizon planning, computer use, memory—are the next frontier for RL-trained agents.
The verifiers library makes building RL-trainable agents as simple as building a normal agent loop with an OpenAI-compatible API.
SFT warm-up from synthetic data generated by frontier APIs lowers the barrier for RL on small models, and debugging can happen before RL using standard API calls.
Those who RL open models well for their tasks will build moats beyond wrapper APIs; the barrier to entry is now just a couple of GPUs.

sections.title: Introduction: Reasoning and Agents Are the Same Thing
sections.summary: Will Brown introduces himself (Prime Intellect) and states his thesis: reasoning and agents are not separate topics but fundamentally the same thing, connected through RL.

sections.title: RL Now Works at Scale
sections.summary: DeepSeek surprised people by showing RL works at scale with few tweaks. Big labs (OpenAI o3) are betting on RL compute for progress. o3 is a naturally agentic model whose value is tool use in complex settings. RL makes systems robust where generic LLM APIs go off the rails.

sections.title: RL Is Complicated but Worth It
sections.summary: Verl's architecture and GRPO from DeepSeek Math paper are complex. But people who RL open models for their tasks will gain a huge advantage and build moats. The field needs to make RL feasible for startups and individual researchers, not just big labs.

sections.title: Agent Products Succeed Because of RL
sections.summary: Agent products (Claude Code, Devon, Manis, o3, Deep Research) work because models were RL'd in similar settings. Claude is good at coding agents because it was RL'd on code. o3 was trained to do image-cropping with tools. The recipe: RL a model to do the task you want.

sections.title: Building Agents Is Canonical RL
sections.summary: Building agents (harness, environment, tools, iteration) maps to canonical RL: policies, actions, states, rewards, transition probabilities. Tuning prompts and harnesses is 'RL by hand.'

sections.title: RL Algorithms: Advantage, GRPO, PPO, DPO
sections.summary: RL estimates advantage from branching rollouts. GRPO is a middle ground: efficient, simple, with forking via sampling. DPO lacks fine-grained advantage estimation. PPO has it but is expensive.

sections.title: Too Many Papers; Focus on Tools and Real Problems
sections.summary: Too many RL papers with sensationalist titles create noise. Brown advises focusing on tools, environments, real-world problems. MCP is simply tools—giving LLMs the ability to interact with systems.

sections.title: Real-World Tasks vs Benchmarks and Reward Hacking
sections.summary: Most RL codebases target math and code because they are easy to evaluate; Brown admits his viral GSM8K snippet contributed to this. Real-world tasks are messier. Reward hacking is fundamentally an eval design problem: you want the task to be easier to do honestly than to hack, so models follow the path of least resistance toward what you actually care about.

sections.title: Rubrics and LLM-as-Judge for Ambiguous Tasks
sections.summary: Generator-verifier gaps exist on a spectrum. Promising direction: break ambiguous tasks into pieces and use LLMs as subroutines in evaluation—LLM-as-judge on steroids, possibly with specialized trained judge models. Brown uses 'rubric' as an umbrella for reward models, reward functions, and LLM-as-judge. DeepSeek's paper on reward models generating rubrics on the fly and a recent creative writing paper show this works for nuanced evaluation.

sections.title: Multi-Turn Agentic Systems as the Frontier
sections.summary: Multi-turn is where the field is headed: agentic search, tool calls, software, games, long-horizon planning, computer use, memory. Scaling on tool calls lets you solve harder problems. Conceptual pieces: environments are harnesses, rewards are evals, tasks are prompts, policy is an LM API.

sections.title: Verifiers Toolkit and Wordle Demo
sections.summary: Brown introduces his open-source verifiers library (on pip), which makes building RL-trainable agents as simple as building a normal agent loop with an OpenAI-compatible API. The rollout function is a simple while-loop with a client object. A Wordle agent demo on a 7B model illustrates the approach, with rewards for solving and for efficiency. SFT warm-up from synthetic data generated by frontier APIs helps bootstrap small models before RL, and environments double as debuggable eval loops.

sections.title: Efficiency, Lowering Barriers, and Closing
sections.summary: Brown highlights efficiency engineering—fully async computation, off-policy training, simultaneous trainer and inference—so users don't have to worry about batching. The goal is lowering barriers so more people can experiment with RL for agents on a couple of GPUs. Brown closes by noting Prime Intellect sells GPUs.

SFT warm-up workflow: use frontier API models to generate synthetic data, SFT on it, then do RL.
limitations: RL is complicated—Verl expects understanding of a large architecture with many moving parts.
Best practices for RL outside big labs remain a research topic.
Too many RL papers with sensationalist titles make it hard to distinguish important work from noise.
Implementation details vary across papers, making generalization difficult.
Most RL codebases are set up for math and code tasks because they are easy to evaluate, but real-world tasks are messier.
Reward hacking is a real and persistent risk; building good evals where honest completion is easier than gaming remains hard.
Rubric-based evaluation with LLMs as subroutines is still early-stage with only preliminary signs it works.
Efficiency challenges in RL training (async, off-policy, batching) remain significant engineering work.
